articles.text: Last week the Post covered events that occurred in or that were relevant to Piedmont schools from January through May 2024. The chronology stopped for the summer break. It was also a time that coincided with the end of teacher salary negotiations. Education in Piedmont spans all ages, from preschool to adult school, and its importance cannot be overstated. The following is the second half of the chronology which aims to recount “how we got here,” and should orient the reader to be all caught up for the new year. Today, Wednesday, January 8, 2025, marks the first day back at school after the winter break for Piedmont teachers, students, administrators, and CSEA classified staff, and a new chapter, entitled 2025 begins. JUNE June 1: The Wildwood Dads Club’s softball team, the Wild Things, won the annual Buzz Redford, Tri-School Softball Tournament. June 12: Piedmont’s school board officially ratified new teacher contracts at the school board meeting, which run through the 2025-26 school year. June 12: Piedmont’s Title IX Task Force announced that Piedmont High School had an equal number of boys and girls playing on sports teams. This metric of equity represented the countless hours of hard work put in by parents, board members and student-athletes advocating for girls in sports. June 26: An increase in enrollment of approximately 100 students for the 2024-25 year was projected in a school board meeting. The upward change in the enrollment trajectory bucked the trend of declining enrollment seen recent years. August 14: Four school board candidates submitted papers to run in November elections. Michael Malione, Susy Struble, and Max Roman were on the ballot for three seats with Victoria Rosenbaum. Soon after, Rosenbaum endorsed the other three and unofficially withdrew her candidacy. articles.text: Gardens for a Changing Planet discussion on Jan. 15 Piedmont Garden Club welcomes the community to attend a discussion by Dr. Ari Novy, President and CEO of the San Diego Botanic Garden, on “Gardens for a Changing Planet: Towards a 21st Century Botanic Garden”. He will be the guest speaker on January 15 at 9:30 a.m. at Piedmont Community Hall. Botanic gardens are more than just beautiful public parks. They play important roles in plant science and conservation. Novy, an internationally recognized leader in the horticultural world, will show how botanic gardens are adapting as the climate changes, He will share how these important green spaces are the sites of research into medicinal, native, and food and agricultural plants. In addition to his role at the Garden, Novy is an active researcher, holding an appointment as Adjunct Associate Professor at Salk Institute for Biological Studies. He is the founding co-chair of the Food and Agriculture Professional Section of the American Public Gardens Association and has served on task forces and advisory panels for diverse groups including the White House Council on Environmental Quality, the Cornell Alliance for Science, Botanic Garden Conservation International, Rock Creek National Park, the Garden Club of America, the European and Mediterranean Plant Protection Organization, and many others. In 2024, he became an honorary Dr. Ari Novy, President and CEO of the San Diego Botanic Garden member of the Garden Club of America. Piedmont Garden Club was founded in 1923 and has been a part of the Garden Club of America since 1926. Piedmont Garden Club members meet monthly to learn about garden-related topics including garden and floral design, garden photography, horticulture and environmental conservation. articles.text: At-risk Pittie mix Potpie is hoping the new year will bring him a new home. Oakland Animal Services staff say this big boy of 70 pounds is a true softie. He’s a playful, affectionate dog who loves to wiggle and bounce around with excitement and show off his silly side. While 4-year-old Potpie has had minimal training, he’s eager to please and is motivated by treats, making him an excellent candidate for positive reinforcement training. He knows the all-important sit command, takes treats gently, and is working on leash manners. He would get on with a dog who matches his gentle play style, or as your one and only pooch. Potpie would be an affectionate companion and happily sit by your side for some love. Come meet Potpie at Oakland Animal Services this Thursday from 12-7 p.m., or Meet Potpie, an at-risk Pittie mix. this Friday, Saturday, or Sunday between 12 and 3 p.m. Potential adopters with a child younger than 12 or a dog that weighs 25 pounds more or less than Potpie must bring them to the shelter for the meeting. For more information, contact Piedmont resident Jessica McDevitt at jessicamcdev@ gmail.com.

articles.text: The League of Women Voters of Piedmont invites community members to an Open House this Sunday, January 12, at 3:00 p.m. at the Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue at Bonita Ave. This free event is an opportunity to meet local League leaders and members, learn about the organization’s projects and programs, and discover ways to get involved in fostering informed and active participation in democracy. The Open House will feature: • Networking: Connect with like-minded individuals committed to making a difference. • Program Plans for 2025: Learn about the League’s advocacy efforts, voter education programs, and community engagement activities. • Volunteer Opportunities: Explore how you can contribute to voter empowerment and civic education. Light refreshments will be served. The Open House will highlight the importance of local engagement in addressing today’s pressing issues. RSVPs are encouraged but not required. articles.text: Tyler Kintz, Construction Superintendent, examines plans at the Dispatch Center construction site. Piedmont city staff gave an informational update at the City Council meeting on Monday, January 6, with updates for the ongoing construction of Piedmont’s 9-1-1 emergency dispatch center. The presentation was given by Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales and Police Chief Jeremy Bowers, According to their report the project has encountered no significant delays and its budget remains on track. Building security and services have been maintained despite a 75% reduction in floor space during the construction process. The project, which started in June 2024, will relocate the dispatch center into the space that formerly served jointly as the City’s Emergency Operations Center and the Police Department’s conference and interview room. Dispatch functions as the nerve center for the Piedmont community’s access to public safety services, fielding over 13,000 calls annually for the Police and Fire Departments. According to the City, the former space was severely undersized, unable to accommodate modern technologies, and located in an area that has not been seismically retrofitted. Additionally, the project includes infrastructure upgrades that benefit the entire Police Department, including an independent electrical system with a backup generator that can provide power for the entire building. Since the construction began last June, concrete has been poured throughout the interior, and for the patio space. articles.text: A quick note of advice: undersell your aspirations As soon as that dreaded clock ticks into place, people scramble to write down their resolutions as if their life depends on their ability to best predict the goals they won’t follow through with. It’s a running joke throughout lifestyle magazines and the New York Times that New Year resolutions are rarely reached as a universal truth. So, what’s the point of “writing resolutions” as an official way to celebrate the New Year? For me, New Years represents a fresh start – the opportunity to become a better version of the person I’ve become over the past twelve months. I believe we put too much pressure on ourselves to accomplish unreasonable goals leading only to the guilt that we reap from not following through on our promises to ourselves. This creates an invisible barrier that if we don’t completely overhaul our lives, we’re complete failures. There’s a reason why only about 25 percent of people stick with their resolutions after just 30 days, and only nine percent who stay with their goals throughout the year. According to the Pew Research Centre, around 79% of resolution makers have one resolution centered on diet or health, often long-term goals. People are so afraid of even attempting to tackle overly ambitious goals that they become frustrated and ultimately give up on their long-term aims. So, what’s the alternative? Everyone is ready to create meaningful change in their life, to turn over a new leaf and feel the beauty of a fresh start. If you’re one of the nine per cent who feels they can stick to a resolution, that’s great. That works for you, and you’re creating change that helps you become a better version of yourself. Unfortunately for a large majority of people, sticking to your resolution is too overwhelming. Even if you’re adamant about writing out your resolutions, let me offer a quick note of advice: undersell your aspirations. Scale back, look at your goals and ask, ‘Is this honestly, truly achievable by me?’. Even better, ditch the resolutions entirely. What I propose: quarterly goals. Small, achievable steps you can take every quarter, every three months. You’ll find that by cutting down the time span, you can also reflect on your goals at the end of each period and see what worked and what didn’t It might allow you to create more attainable or ambitious goals for the next quarters. This forces you to choose a smaller timeframe, allowing for smaller, more manageable goals. You can even go smaller monthly resolutions, or even weekly. Consistency is, as it often is, key to maintaining a path that is both possible and rewarding. With this article, I hope to shed some light on reality. While often cruel it can be a way to find more fulfilling ways of accomplishing your goals. By setting your goals and reaching higher aspirations for the next quarter. Whatever you choose to do, I wish you all the best of success and hope that you can achieve those goals this year. Daisy Seymour is a Piedmont teen who got really frustrated she didn’t manage to reach her resolutions last year.
articles.title: A look at the failure of New Year resolutions

articles.text: Highlanders enter January with a 10-1 record Piedmont High’s girls’ basketball team continued its great start to the season, improving its record to 10-1, They recently beat Clayton Valley Charter 61-52 in overtime at the Sabrina Ionescu 20 Showcase at Carondelet in Concord on Friday, January 3. They also won three of four games at the San Diego Holiday Classic tournament at Torrey Pines HS from December 26-30. In tournament, results they opened with a 72-26 win over Canyon of Anaheim, lost 68-55 to Mission Hills of San Marcos, beat Cal High of San Ramon 74-50, and won 51-45 over Oak Ridge of El Dorado Hills to close. Freshman Jenelle Solis made the San Diego Holiday Classic All-Tournament team. “I feel like we’re watching the growth of the team right before our eyes. We’re starting to meet teams that match us. It showed a lot tonight [against Clayton Valley],” coach Bryan Gardere said. The last group of games marked the official start for Senior Briana Webb is proving to be a vital part of this year’s team. She had a double-double against California. transfer students Briana Webb and Taylor White. Both come to Piedmont after spending time at Moreau HS in Hayward. “It’s about our chemistry; we’re really coming together as a team,” said White. “When we’re down, we pull each other up. We have great potential, we’re young but we’re mighty. Tonight was really about defense and focusing on their best player.” . “I think we’re coming together really well,” added Webb. “I’m trying to help out with communication because a lot of the girls are so young, so I try to speak up and help them figure things out with their roles and where to be. My approach is to play well defensively because if I can get steals, force turnovers, and get rebounds, I know it will transfer to the offensive side.” In the victory over Clayton Valley Charter, Piedmont trailed by 11 points at the half but rallied for a strong second half performance. “We’re playing together and not forcing anything. Coach gave us a hard talk at halftime. We didn’t play scared and just stayed together, said Andrea Martin. 61-52 over Clayton Valley in overtime Piedmont trailed 17-11 by the end of the first quarter and 32-21 by halftime. The comeback began in the third quarter with PHS taking its first lead of the game, 33-32, with 3:25 left in the third, but Clayton Valley quickly got back ahead to start the fourth period leading 38-36. There were three lead changes in the fourth quarter, including White hitting a 3-pointer with 50 seconds left to go up 47-45, but CV scored the tying basket with six seconds left to force overtime. Although CVC took an initial 48-47 lead in overtime on a free throw, Savannah Dennig put Piedmont back up 49-48 and the Highlanders never looked back., They scored five unanswered points to lead 54-48 with 2:15 left. CV clawed away to make it 54-52 with 1:39 remaining, but it was their last score of the game. Piedmont closed it out with seven more points, including four by Martin. Final scorers: Martin had 23 points, Webb had 13 points, White had 12 points, Solis had five points, and Dennig had four. 51-45 win over Oak Ridge Piedmont held a narrow 11-6 lead and went up 24-13 by halftime. Oak Ridge outscored PHS 17-10 in the third to clip away at PHS’ lead 34-30, but the Highlanders held on with 17 points to OR’s 15. Final stats: Martin led with 17 points, seven rebounds, one assist, three steals, and four blocks. Solis scored 16 points, five rebounds, five assists, and one block. Webb had eight points, eight rebounds, and two assists. Dennig scored three points, three rebounds, and one assist. White had six points, six rebounds, two assists, and one steal. 74-50 blowout of California Piedmont t railed 19-16 through the first quarter, but went up in the second quarter to lead 33-29 by halftime. PHS then outscored the Grizzlies 19-7 in the third to take a commanding 52-36 lead into the fourth, adding 22 more points in the final going. Final stats: Martin scored 24 points, 10 rebounds, two assists, two steals, and one block. Solis had 19 points, seven assists, three Staff Photos Sophomore Taylor White is making an impact in her first games with Piedmont. rebounds, and one steal. Webb had 16 points, 12 rebounds, two assists, and two steals. Dennig had six points, two rebounds, two assists, and a steal. White had seven points, seven rebounds, four assists, and four steals. 68-55 loss to Mission Hills In Piedmont’s only loss if the season, Mission Hills led 20-15 through the first quarter and 28-25 by halftime. MH then scored 23 in the third to lead 51-36 entering the fourth, scoring 17 more in the final quarter. Final stats: Martin had 21 points, eight rebounds, one assist, one steal, and one block. Dennig had four points, one rebound and assist. Solis scored 14 points and six assists. Shakila Zuberi had two points and three rebounds. White had 10 points and three rebounds, Webb had four points, five rebounds, and three assists. 72-26 drubbing of Canyon Piedmont led 25-10 through the first and 49-13 by halftime. With a running clock, PHS led 61-22 through the third and added 11 more in the final going. Final stats: Solis led with 29 points, six assists, and three steals. Webb had 25 points, four rebounds, three assists, and two steals. Martin had eight points, six rebounds, two assists, five steals, and a block. Dennig had two points, three rebounds, three assists, and two steals. White had six points, six rebounds, two assists, and one steal. articles.text: PHS beats El Cerrito, loses to St. Joseph in OT Staff Photos Dillon Casey scored 24 points against El Cerrito and 25 against St. Joseph. The Highlanders’ boys’ basketball team split its first two games of the New Year, defeating El Cerrito 65-57 in the Gauchos’ home gym on Monday, January 6, and losing a heartbreaker 70-68 in overtime to St. Joseph at Binks Rawlings Gym on Saturday, January 8. Their recent win snapped a three-game losing streak and brough its record to 6-5. The loss to St. Joe came after the Pilots sank a buzzer-beater to force overtime, followed by another buzzer-beater basket to win the game. “We’re a young team that hasn’t been in a lot of situations like St. Joe. We had some jitters in the first quarter, but we were good for most of the game,” said coach Ben Spencer. Piedmont did well to deal with an aggressive press by El Cerrito for the entire second half. “Despite being a bit tired from that overtime game. We handled the ball pretty well in the third quarter and not too many turnovers. It wasn’t until the fourth quarter until their press started making an impact. With a young team that’s going to happen. We let them play through it and they knew what they had to do. These games will get us ready for league play and the postseason,” Spencer said. Monday’s game was also a strong performance by sophomore Lucian Fang-Ring, who hit two 3-pointers in the third quarter and another in the fourth to help put the game away. After getting limited minutes toward the end of his freshman season, Fang-Ring is in his first season of a full varsity role. “It felt like our energy was falling away and I wanted to shoot the big shot. It feels good to have the upperclassmen trust me, It’s good to bounce back and snap out of that three-game losing streak,” Fang-Ring said following their win over El Cerrito. Piedmont looks ahead to the start of a busy week. They begin their Western Alameda County Conference schedule tomorrow, January 9 with a game against San Leandro, then a game at University in San Francisco on January 11, and a game at home against Bishop O’Dowd on Tuesday, January 14. 65-57 win vs. over El Cerrito Piedmont trailed early before taking the lead at 11-10 with 1:02 left in the first quarter when Ravi Silverberg converted a threepoint play. They never relinquished their advantage from then on, ending the opening quarter with a narrow 14-13 lead. Sophomore Lucian Fang-Ring had a big second-half in Piedmont’s win over El Cerrito. In the second quarter, Silverberg opened things with another three-point play after Fang-Ring nabbed an offensive rebound and sending a slick pass to Silverberg under the rim for the lay-up and foul. After El Cerrito made a free throw to make it 17-14, PHS went on an 8-1 scoring run to take a 25-15 lead. Dillon Casey knocked down a 3-pointer on an assist from Silverberg to close the quarter, making it 28-19 at the half. Piedmont opened the third quarter with a 7-2 scoring run to build a 35-22 advantage. The Gauchos cut the deficit to four points at 38-34, but Fang-Ring hit a big 3-pointer to make it 41-34. After four more points by El Cerrito, P.J. Brayer hit another 3-pointer to end the quarter, leading 44-38. In the fourth quarter, PHS opened with a 6-1 scoring run with a 3-pointer by Casey and a three-point play by Fang-Ring to lead 50-41. Fang-Ring helped put the game away when assisting Silverberg for a 3-pointer, hitting a three of his own, then assisting Silverberg again for a three with 1:55 remaining to make it 62-50. Final scorers: Casey led with 24 points, Silverberg had 17, Fang-Ring had 14, Brayer scored eight, and Beach Lorin had two. 70-68 loss in OT to St. Joseph Piedmont led 20-13 by the end of the first quarter and clung to a two-point 30-28 lead by halftime. The Highlanders slightly extended their advantage to 48-45 in the third quarter, but St. Joe tied the game at the very-last second of the fourth quarter to force overtime at 60-60. In overtime, the Pilots converted another buzzer-beater for the 70-68 win. Final scorers: Silverberg led with 26 points, Casey had 25, Brayer scored eight, Fang-Ring had seven, and Emmett Asulin had two. articles.text: The San Francisco Ballet premiere of Sir Kenneth MacMillan’s Manon opens the company’s 2024-25 Repertory Season on Friday, January 24. Inspired by the 1731 novel Manon Lescaut by Abbé Prévost, Manon is considered one of MacMillan’s most notable and widely-celebrated works. The ballet chronicles the rise and fall of its titular heroine, beginning near Paris and ending in New Orleans. The three-act ballet was first performed by The Royal Ballet in London in 1974 with Antoinette Sibley and Anthony Dowell in principal roles. “MacMillan was an artist who infused novelty and depth into his choreography,” San Francisco Ballet Artistic Director Tamara Rojo said. “Manon exemplifies how he brought new life to a classic story, transforming it into a timeless narrative.” Principal casting for Manon includes Dores André, Jasmine Jimison, Sasha De Sola, with Nikisha Fogo as Manon, and Harrison James, Max Cauthorn, and Aaron Robison as des Grieux. San Francisco Ballet welcomes principal guest artist Alban Lendorf to the War Memorial Opera House stage for select performances as des Grieux. The War Memorial Opera House bars will serve a specialty cocktail inspired by the themes of Manon and 18th-century France. Manon will be performed through February 1. articles.text: The San Francisco Botanical Garden in Golden Gate Park will host an artist reception with photographer Mark Citret on Saturday, February 8. Citret, a San Francisco native, began photographing in 1968 and in the 1980’s produced a large body of work titled “Unnatural Wonders”, which is his personal survey of architecture in national parks. The February 8 event highlights the artists’ latest collection of works, entitled Structural Beauty: Photographs of the San Francisco Botanical Garden. In this new exhibition, Citret captures the physical beauty of plants through black and white photographs, his preferred medium. Citret received both his BA and MA in Art from San Francisco State University, and has taught photography at the University of California Berkeley Extension since 1982. Structural Beauty: Photographs of the San Francisco Botanical Garden is on exhibit at the Helen Crocker Russell Library in the San Francisco Botanical Garden February 8 through May, 2025. The reception is from 2 p.m. to 4 p.m. and is free to the public. Reservations are encouraged. Visit https://gggp.org/event/artistreception-with-mark-citret/ for more details. articles.text: Treasure Island Museum will host an expert-panel discussion on Yerba Buena Island’s natural history this Saturday, January 11 at 10 a.m. Yerba Buena Island is the second largest natural island in San Francisco Bay, and its development and restoration is an on-going and multi-phase effort, much like the larger, man-made Treasure Island. Yerba Buena Island was historically used as a naval base and training center and its native ecosystems have been replaced by invasive species. Significant and biodiverse natural areas still remain, and ongoing redevelopment of Yerba Buena Island and Treasure Island provided the opportunity to restore native ecology. Both islands have been planted with over 50 species of native plants, including flora and fauna that are native to the ecosystem. According to Treasure Island Museum staff, the design and planning for these spaces involved a unique and collaborative effort between developers, the City of San Francisco, ecologists, local nurseries and landscape architects. Peter Brastow, from the San Francisco Environment Department and Will Benge, Senior Associate with CMG Landscape Architecture will be onsite to discuss restoration efforts. Tickets are free, but reservation is required. Visit https:// www.treasureislandmuseum.org/ event-details/restoration-of-yerba-buena-island-weaving-ecology-with-place-and-infrastructure to register. articles.text: “Elio & Stefano Ciol: Into The Light,” an exhibit showcasing the work of Italian father-son photographers Elio and Stefano Ciol, is on view at Museo Italo America in San Francisco now through February 2. Both photographers, hailing from Casarsa della Delizia in the Italian region of Friuli Venezia Giulia, are known for works that highlight their masterful use of light, balance of geometric lines and angles, and impeccable photographic composition. These three essential aspects enabled the father-son pair to create visually captivating and highly structured pieces that stand the test of time. Elio, born in 1929, lived his formative years during Nazi occupation and is now renowned as one of the foremost European masters of landscape photography. Many of his predominantly black and white shots have been featured in over one hundred solo exhibitions. “Elio & Stefano Ciol: Into The Light” showcases a collection spanning over sixty years. Museum hours are Tuesday through Saturday, 12:00 p.m. to 4:00 p.m. and Sunday, 10:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. The exhibit is free on Thursdays. Museo Italo Americano is the first museum in the United States devoted exclusively to Italian and Italian-American art and culture, located in San Francisco’s historic Fort Mason. Visit https:// sfmuseo.org/exhibition/elio-andstefano-ciol-into-the-light/ to learn more. Patrons view “Elio & Stefano Ciol: Into The Light” at Museo Italo Americano in San Francisco.

articles.text: Thursday, January 16, 7:00 p.m. Michael Stehr Art Lecture Join art historian Michael Stehr as he discusses the importance of the current show at San Francisco’s Legion of Honor, entitled Mary Cassatt at Work. Too often dismissed as a sentimental painter of mothers and children, Mary Cassatt (1844– 1926) was in fact a modernist pioneer. Her paintings, pastels, and prints are characterized by restless experimentation and change. Cassatt was the only American to join the French Impressionists, first exhibiting with the group at Degas’ invitation in 1879, and quickly emerged as a key member of the movement. Some friends invited my string Quartet to play background music before the banquet. That was our pleasure, to say the least. And then we feasted. The entire meal was memorable, but here are a couple of items that you can make yourself: The main course was roasted quail with truffles, but maybe you could try to make the first course. Above a creamy bed of cauliflower was a mixture of wild mushrooms. If you don’t want cream of cauliflower, I would recommend a bed of polenta. Sauté some wild mushrooms and sprinkle them above the bed of cream cauliflower or polenta. The banquet featured 10 carefully selected wines which served to increase the delight of the foods. At the end was a great surprise – a Madeira wine vintage 1908. I wonder if royalty ever ate as well. articles.text: A scene from Disney/Pixar’s Inside Out 2 The genius of Pixar Animation Studios resides with its spot-on sense of audience. It consistently demonstrates imaginative storytelling featuring characters that resonate, plus plots that compel. Clearly, Pixar also possesses a deep bench of extraordinary animators who, in feature after feature, create vibrant, rich images. I would judge that Inside Out 2 represents all of the above, and surely must have been a challenge for both the writers and the animators. Riley Anderson, previously a tween in Inside Out, finds herself on the precarious cusp of adolescence and all that it entails. Where once life was relatively calm, involving lingering residuals of childhood, well, being a newbie teen can feel as if you are abruptly unmoored, adrift, often steeped in uncertainty. Early cartographers labeled those area yet to be explored as places where “there be dragons.” Indeed. Riley’s parents are, of course, one barometer of her surprising mood swings and unpredictable intensity. What is the sound of a bedroom door slamming? Or how to understand the “DO NOT ENTER” sign on the door? Of course, most often stories that depict the onset of teendom focus on the external stuff that features a panoply of new behaviors, as if this stranger is taking a ride on a roller coaster or is engaged in bumper cars. Both are easy metaphors for unanticipated emotions suddenly made manifest. But Pixar has done something extraordinary in its storytelling explanation of Riley’s conflicted reactions: relying on the remarkable license offered by animation, they have used personification to depict a deep bench of characters, each an inspired representation of Riley’s familiar emotions as well as those rookies who have only recently appeared in the lineup. To make all of the above interesting, Riley and her buds are off to hokey camp where her veteran and new squad of feelings will be put to the test. Taking the familiar lead is Joy (Amy Poehler), calm and caring, who has always been in charge of a NASA-like emotions central panel. That is until Anxiety (Maya Hawke), frazzled, bug-eyed, wild hair, red everything steps up to reaction central, and begins to dominate, opening the door to Embarrassment, Envy, mixed with the old school Sadness, Anger, Fear, and even Ennui (lassitude). Riley confronts her desire to be popular, to be liked by the older hockey camp girls, while the word “cool” swirls. Plus an confronts an unfamiliar desire to fit in and so transforms herself and thereby gain the approval of those who have already achieved “cool.” This results in Riley becoming a person that her friends, and ultimately even Riley herself, no longer recognize. Meanwhile, back at the emotive control panel, a struggle develops between Joy, and the frenetic, unrelenting Anxiety who is buttressed by Envy. Ultimately, the question begged is: will Riley return to her core values, and to her faithful friends? Or will Anxiety prevail, causing Riley to abandon the person she truly is as personified by Joy, and instead choose trendy popularity and facile coolness? Regarding the writers, choosing hockey camp as the setting is inspired. It is a kaleidoscope of new challenges for Riley. And regarding the teen vernacular/ interactions it’s perfect. Considering perfect, the animation is remarkable, the intensity of hockey nailed. Plus the emotions (determination, disappointment, desire to win not only the game but the approbation of the team), are exceptional. As am aside, Inside Out 2 was nominated for a Golden Globe award, and though it didn’t win, the Golden Globes are often a reliable precursor to the coming Oscars. Inside Out 2. Pixar–Disney animation. Directed by Kelsey Mann. Starring Amy Poehler, Maya Hawke, Phyllis Smith. 1 hr., 36 min. Rated PG. Released in 2024. Streaming on prime/Disney+.

articles.text: From the world renowned Japanese Studio Ghibli, The Secret World of Arrietty was co-written by two of its principal storytellers, Hiromasa Yonebayashi and Hayao Miyazaki. It is based on the famed children’s fantasy novels titled The Borrowers, by British writer Mary Norton. Set in 1950s England, the borrowers are a race of teacup size people who make their confortable if diminutive home under the floorboards of an old fashioned English cottage. At the center of this delightful narrative is Arrietty, an adventurous 14-year-old girl (Bridget Mendler) who lives with her mother, Homily (Amy Poehler), and father, Pod (Will Arnett). They survive day to day by “borrowing” bits of food and objects from the “human beans” who live above the floorboards. It is important to know that a sacrosanct rule, even law, is that a Borrower must, at all cost, never reveal him or herself to a “bean.” Should that happen, alas, the Borrowers, they believe, are put in real danger and must find a new residence. But then a sickly 12-yearold boy, Shawn (David Henrie), comes to stay at his aunt’s home to convalesce. He is keen-eyed and curious. Meanwhile, Arrietty and her father go on a mission above the floorboards to borrow a cube of sugar, an adventure to be sure for she is fascinated by the sheer size of the bean world, something she views in all its gigantic splendor and potential danger. But, as it turns out, she is also drawn into Shawn’s personal world and is soon discovered by the bean boy. Surprisingly these two most disparate characters fashion a friendship and a bond of trust. Of course, one of the beans, an elderly housekeeper, Hara (Carol Burnett), is ever on guard, intent on ridding the bean’s home of any “pests.” The danger to Arrietty and family is palpable. The Secret is a wonderful tale, lush and beautiful, hand drawn animé that brings to life this contrasting world of Borrowers and beans. It is also a coming-ofage story featuring a strong and courageous newbie-teenage girl who years to expand her horizons above the floorboards and exhibits a focused fearlessness and kindness, qualities that are endearing. This film tells a tender story and is a visual stunner while avoiding the fantastical, extraordinary, shape-shifting characters that are often part of the Ghibli world. The Secret World of Arrietty. Voters later passed a bond issue to reimburse them. The walkers’ first destination on the first Wednesday of 2025 was the Piedmont Park History Trail marker summary in front of the Piedmont Veterans Memorial Building. There they learned that when Piedmont celebrated its 100th anniversary in 2007 a public/private partnership was developed to preserve the history of Piedmont Park and to create a self-guided walking park tour with nine markers. The walkers went to the first marker just up Vista Avenue past the City Hall in the shaded, somewhat secluded courtyard at its right front. They read the Last Original Park Bench marker with a photo of a rustic wood bench near the spring’s grotto. The group exited the courtyard and went down Vista to Bonita Avenue, then turned up Magnolia Avenue with the second marker at the Exedra. This one told how Blair built the Piedmont Springs Hotel. Next, the walkers went behind the Exedra to the upper edge of the park where a marker told the story of Havens opening his Piedmont Springs Park in 1898. The walkers continued past the Community Hall to the Japanese Tea House. This is not the original tea house that Havens built in 1907 as a park attraction. When the City acquired the park in the 1920s, the tea house was torn down to make room for a new civic center master plan. In 1976 when the Leander Redmon estate at Hillside and Magnolia Avenues was razed to build the new Piedmont Middle School its tea house was donated to the City of Piedmont was moved to its current site. The group’s next stop was outside the park tennis courts. Here Havens had built a world class art museum in 1907. The walkers went behind the Community Hall into the park and took the lower path that followed Bushy Dell Creek to the Cascade marker. This was “a lush tropical paradise” and an artificial waterfall. The next stop was the marker for the Sulphur Springs Grotto which told how Mark Twain was there in 1867. Makes 6 very large biscuits INGREDIENTS • 1½ cups all-purpose flour • 1½ cups cake flour • 1 tablespoon baking powder • ½ teaspoon baking soda • 1 teaspoon table salt • 8 tablespoons unsalted butter, cut into ½” pieces and softened • 4 tablespoons pork leaf lard, cut into ½” pieces (Substitute vegetable shortening if you insist) • 11̸8 cup buttermilk INSTRUCTIONS 1. Adjust an oven rack to upper-middle position and heat oven to 425°F. Butter a 9” round cake pan. 2. Combine flours, baking powder, baking soda and salt in a large bowl. Rub the butter and shortening into flour mixture until it resembles coarse meal. Stir in buttermilk until combined. 3. Use a buttered ½ cup measuring cup or scoop to transfer 6 heaping portions of dough into prepared pan. Place 5 portions around the perimeter and 1 in the center. 4. Bake until puffed and golden brown, 20 – 25 minutes. Cool in pan for 10 minutes then transfer to a wire rack.
